title: StructureComposition
description: How one building is put together, so a player can name it from across the valley without reading a label. One entry per building id. See docs/RENDER_25D.md. Nothing here reaches the simulation: `standing` is a drawing number and cover has its own model (Cover.Stature) — a taller drawing must never change a fight.

id.description: The building id this describes. Must name an entry in buildings.json — a composition for a building that does not exist is a drawing nothing will ever ask for.

standing.description: Wall height in map units, before the roof. The number the plan view could never say: a hut is about 0.9, a longhouse 1.1, a granary 1.8, a watchtower 3.4.

roof.description: How the top is closed off. The set StructureVariant.Roofline already draws.

fabric.description: What the wall face is made of. `open` is a roof on posts with no wall — a work lean-to, a market row. Each maps to a Cover.Substance for the simulation, and that mapping is what keeps cover unchanged: a brick wall stops a shaft exactly as a stone one does.

trim.description: What frames the face — the timber crucks across daub, the stone quoins at a brick corner.

rooftop.description: What stands on the roof. The set StructureVariant.Rooftop already draws.

attachments.description: What stands beside the building and says what it is from across the valley: a charcoal heap, drying racks, an anvil under an awning, crates on a loading step. This is the field that stops five `plant` buildings being one building drawn five times. Two or three; six is a junkyard. Every value must be a part the renderer draws — a new part is a code change, and then every building may have it (rule 92).

yard.description: What the ground does around it.

accent.description: The one thing allowed to be warm in a bone-on-slate world. At most one per building, or the town becomes a fairground.
